name: max_retries 0 sends exactly one request on a governed operation
description:
`maxRetries = 0` is a legal spelling of "no retries — exactly one attempt", not a request to send nothing. Go (#180) and Ruby (#181) each had a pre-check loop that broke out before the first send whenever the cap was 0 and raised "Request failed after 0 retries" for a request it never made; both now floor the cap at one, and this case is the cross-language pin those two unit tests could not be.

`GetBoard` is governed: it carries a `retry.max` of 3 in behavior-model.json and 503 is in its declared `retry_on` set, so every retrying SDK would otherwise make three attempts here. A single 503 is queued deliberately: every runner answers past the end of the queue with a 500, and 500 is ALSO in the declared set, so an SDK that retried keeps going to its cap and `requestCount: 1` cannot pass vacuously — it fails on the count either way.

**Strength is not uniform across the runners, and this fixture does not pretend otherwise.** Go and Ruby consult the budget BEFORE the first request (pre-check loops), so a zero cap is a real regression guard there. Rust floors the cap in the builder itself (`max_attempts(0)` reads as one) and clamps each route's budget under it. Kotlin and TypeScript consult the budget only after the first response, so a cap of 0 and of 1 are observably identical in those two; in Kotlin the client cap is a ceiling on the per-operation budget, and in TypeScript there is no numeric cap at all — the override maps to `enableRetry: false`, which is its spelling of the same contract. Swift is the same shape as TypeScript (no numeric cap, `enableRetry`, a loop floored at one) but has no conformance runner yet.
